overview.title: Rank-3 and higher tensors; the three key attributes: rank, shape, dtype
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.subsection: 2.2.4 Rank-3 tensors and higher-rank tensors; 2.2.5 Key attributes
overview.main_topic: Rows and columns of a matrix; building a rank-3 tensor by packing matrices (and rank 4, 5 by packing further); the three attributes that define any tensor: number of axes (rank/`ndim`), shape (tuple of sizes per axis) and data type (`dtype`).
overview.central_idea: Any tensor is completely described by its rank, its shape and its dtype. Higher-rank tensors are built by packing lower-rank ones, and deep learning mostly uses ranks 0 to 4 (5 for video).
overview.importance: Rank, shape and dtype are the three things you check about any tensor before feeding it to a model or debugging a shape error; they are the vocabulary the whole book uses to describe data (p.50) and layer compatibility (p.117). The page also gives the mental image for higher ranks: a cube of numbers, then stacks of cubes.
learning_objectives: Identify rows (first axis) and columns (second axis) of a matrix.
Construct a rank-3 tensor by packing matrices and state its shape, e.g. (3, 3, 5).
Define rank, shape and dtype and read them off any NumPy array (`ndim`, `shape`, `dtype`).
State which ranks are typical in deep learning (0 to 4, up to 5 for video).
prerequisites: Scalars, vectors and matrices as rank-0, 1 and 2 tensors, and the `ndim` attribute (p.46).
The 3 x 5 matrix defined on p.46.

summary:
The page completes the matrix example of p.46: `x.ndim` is `2`. The entries along the first axis are the **rows** and along the second axis the **columns**: `[5, 78, 2, 34, 0]` is the first row and `[5, 6, 7]` the first column.

**2.2.4 Rank-3 tensors and higher-rank tensors.** Packing such matrices into a new array gives a **rank-3 tensor** (3D tensor), which can be pictured as a *cube of numbers*. The example packs three copies of the 3 x 5 matrix, giving `x.ndim == 3`. Packing rank-3 tensors yields a rank-4 tensor, and so on. In deep learning you generally manipulate tensors of rank 0 to 4, up to 5 for video data.

**2.2.5 Key attributes.** A tensor is defined by three key attributes:

- **Number of axes (rank)**: a rank-3 tensor has three axes, a matrix two. Called `ndim` in NumPy, JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch.
- **Shape**: a tuple of integers giving how many dimensions the tensor has along each axis. The matrix example has shape `(3, 5)`, the rank-3 example `(3, 3, 5)`; a vector has a one-element shape such as `(5,)`; a scalar has the empty shape `()`.
- **Data type** (`dtype`): the type of the data in the tensor, e.g. `float16`, `float32`, `float64`, `uint8`, `bool`; in TensorFlow also `string` tensors.

To make this concrete the authors turn back to the MNIST data: the page ends by announcing the reload of the dataset, whose `ndim`, `shape` and `dtype` are inspected on p.48.

paragraphs.excerpt: The entries from the first axis are called the rows, and the entries
paragraphs.what_it_says: After `x.ndim` returns 2 for the matrix of p.46, the authors name its axes: entries along the first axis are rows, along the second axis columns. `[5, 78, 2, 34, 0]` is the first row and `[5, 6, 7]` the first column.
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'Rows' and 'columns' are just the conventional names of axis 0 and axis 1. The first row is `x[0]` (fix the first index), the first column is `x[:, 0]` (fix the second index). The first column's values 5, 6, 7 are the first entries of each of the three rows.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Knowing which axis is which is what lets you read a shape like `(60000, 784)` as 'samples along axis 0, features along axis 1' (p.50), and later lets you pick the right axis for reductions and slicing (p.49).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Axis 0 has length 3 (number of rows), axis 1 has length 5 (number of columns), so the shape is (3, 5) as stated in the Shape bullet below.

terminology.meaning: An entry along the first axis of a matrix: one of its constituent vectors.
An entry along the second axis: the values at one fixed position across all rows.

connections: p.46: the matrix `x` was defined as an array of three 5-entry vectors.
p.49: slicing syntax such as `x[:, 0]` selects along a chosen axis.

paragraphs.excerpt: If you pack such matrices in a new array, you obtain a rank-3 tensor
paragraphs.what_it_says: Packing matrices into a new array produces a rank-3 tensor (3D tensor), visually a cube of numbers. The NumPy example packs three identical 3 x 5 matrices; `x.ndim` is 3.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each packing step adds a new leading axis. The resulting cube has three index directions: which matrix (0-2), which row (0-2), which column (0-4), hence shape (3, 3, 5). This is the same operation that turns a set of 28 x 28 image matrices into the MNIST tensor of shape (60000, 28, 28) (p.48).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Rank-3 tensors are the native format of sequence data (samples, timesteps, features) (p.51) and of grayscale image batches like MNIST; the cube picture is the mental model to carry.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Three indices select an element: `x[i, j, k]` with i the matrix, j the row, k the column; `x[2, 1, 3]` is 35.

terminology.meaning: An array of matrices; a tensor with three axes, picturable as a cube of numbers.

connections: p.48: `train_images` is a rank-3 tensor: 60,000 matrices of 28 x 28 integers.
p.51: timeseries data stored as rank-3 tensors with a time axis at index 1.

paragraphs.excerpt: By packing rank-3 tensors in an array, you can create a rank-4 tensor,
paragraphs.what_it_says: Packing rank-3 tensors gives a rank-4 tensor, and so on. In deep learning one generally manipulates ranks 0 to 4, going up to 5 for video.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The recursion has no upper limit in principle, but in practice the data types of the field fix the ranks: scalars (losses), vectors (single samples, labels), matrices (batches of vectors), rank 3 (sequences, grayscale image batches), rank 4 (colour image batches), rank 5 (video batches).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This sets expectations: you will not meet rank-7 tensors, but you must be comfortable with rank 4, because that is what every convnet in chapter 8 consumes (p.50).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Rank 4 for images: (samples, height, width, channels); rank 5 for video: (samples, frames, height, width, channels) (p.50, p.52).

terminology.meaning: Tensors with four or five axes, used for batches of images and batches of videos respectively.

connections: p.50: the four standard data tensor categories by rank.
p.52: a batch of four video clips as a (4, 240, 144, 256, 3) rank-5 tensor.

paragraphs.excerpt: Number of axes (rank)—For instance, a rank-3 tensor has three axes, and
paragraphs.what_it_says: First key attribute: the number of axes, or rank. A rank-3 tensor has three axes, a matrix two. Called `ndim` in NumPy, JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Rank is the attribute already used on p.46; here it is formalized as one of three defining properties, and the authors note that all major frameworks expose it under the same name, so the knowledge transfers across TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX (chapter 3).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Layers expect inputs of a specific rank (p.117: Dense for rank 2, recurrent for rank 3, Conv2D for rank 4), so checking `ndim` is the first step when a shape error appears.

terminology.meaning: Attribute name for the rank in NumPy, JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch.

connections: p.46: `ndim` introduced with the scalar, vector and matrix examples.
p.117: which layer types fit which tensor ranks.

paragraphs.excerpt: Shape—This is a tuple of integers that describes how many dimensions the
paragraphs.what_it_says: Second key attribute: the shape, a tuple of integers giving how many dimensions the tensor has along each axis. The matrix example has shape (3, 5), the rank-3 example (3, 3, 5); a vector has a single-element shape like (5,); a scalar has the empty shape ().
paragraphs.what_it_means: The shape carries the rank (its length) and the size along every axis; it is the most informative single description of a tensor. Note the Python detail that a one-element tuple needs a trailing comma, `(5,)`, and that `()` is a valid, empty tuple.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Almost every bug in deep learning code is a shape mismatch; the book writes shapes constantly ((60000, 784), (samples, timesteps, features), ...) and the reader must read them fluently. Reshaping (p.58) is the operation that changes shape without changing content.
paragraphs.technical_idea: `len(x.shape) == x.ndim`; the number of elements is the product of the shape entries: 3 x 3 x 5 = 45 for the rank-3 example.

terminology.meaning: Tuple with one integer per axis giving the tensor's size along that axis.

paragraphs.excerpt: Data type (usually called dtype in Python libraries)—This is the type of
paragraphs.what_it_says: Third key attribute: the data type, `dtype`, the type of the data in the tensor: `float16`, `float32`, `float64`, `uint8`, `bool`, and so on. In TensorFlow one also meets `string` tensors.
paragraphs.what_it_means: All entries of a tensor share one type, which fixes how many bits each uses and whether it is integer, floating point, boolean or string. The MNIST images arrive as `uint8` (p.48) and were converted to `float32` on p.44 because that is the type the network computes in.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: dtype determines memory (p.52 computes 425 MB for a float32 video batch), numerical precision, and whether an operation is even allowed (integer division trap on p.44). `float32` is the default workhorse of deep learning.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: `float16` uses 2 bytes per value, `float32` 4, `float64` 8, `uint8` 1; `bool` masks are used for selection; string tensors hold raw text before tokenization.

terminology.meaning: The data type shared by every entry of a tensor.
32-bit floating point, the standard dtype for model inputs and weights.
Unsigned 8-bit integer (0-255), the natural dtype for raw pixel data.

connections: p.44: conversion to float32 before training.
p.52: dtype and memory footprint of a video tensor.

paragraphs.what_it_says: To make the three attributes concrete, the authors return to the MNIST data, starting by loading the dataset again (the code and the inspection of `ndim`, `shape` and `dtype` follow on p.48).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The abstract attributes are about to be read off a real tensor: rank 3, shape (60000, 28, 28), dtype uint8, i.e. 60,000 grayscale matrices of 28 x 28 integers.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It closes the loop with section 2.1: the data you already trained on was a rank-3 uint8 tensor all along.

concepts.name: Number of axes (rank, `ndim`)
concepts.definition: The first key attribute of a tensor: how many axes it has; called `ndim` in NumPy, JAX, TensorFlow and PyTorch.
concepts.intuition: How many nested levels of brackets, or how many indices you need to reach one number.
concepts.technical: A matrix has 2 axes, the page's cube example 3. Equal to `len(shape)`.
concepts.significance: Layer types are matched to ranks (p.117); rank is the first thing to check about an input.
concepts.example: `x.ndim` is 2 for the 3 x 5 matrix and 3 for the packed cube.
concepts.misconception: Rank is not the number of entries along an axis; see the 5D vector warning on p.46.

concepts.name: Shape
concepts.definition: A tuple of integers describing how many dimensions a tensor has along each axis.
concepts.intuition: The size of the box in every direction: 3 rows by 5 columns is (3, 5); three such sheets stacked is (3, 3, 5).
concepts.technical: Length of the tuple = rank; product of entries = number of elements. A vector's shape is `(5,)`, a scalar's is `()`.
concepts.significance: The primary language for describing data and debugging models; every shape in the book, from (60000, 784) to (samples, frames, height, width, channels), is read this way.
concepts.example: The rank-3 example has shape (3, 3, 5): 3 matrices, each 3 rows by 5 columns.
concepts.misconception: `(5)` in Python is just the integer 5; a one-element shape must be written `(5,)`.

concepts.name: Data type (dtype)
concepts.definition: The type of the data contained in a tensor, such as float16, float32, float64, uint8 or bool (and string in TensorFlow).
concepts.intuition: What kind of number each cell holds and how many bits it occupies.
concepts.technical: One dtype per tensor. Determines memory per element, precision, and allowed operations. Neural networks compute in float32 by default; raw images are often uint8.
concepts.significance: Explains why MNIST was converted from uint8 to float32 (p.44) and why large float32 tensors are memory-heavy (p.52).
concepts.misconception: Changing dtype is not free of consequences: casting float32 to uint8 truncates values and casting to float16 loses precision.

concepts.name: Rank-3 and higher-rank tensors
concepts.definition: Tensors obtained by packing matrices (rank 3, a cube of numbers), then packing rank-3 tensors (rank 4), and so on.
concepts.intuition: A cube of numbers, then a row of cubes, then a grid of cubes.
concepts.technical: The page's example: three 3 x 5 matrices packed into a (3, 3, 5) tensor, `ndim` 3. Deep learning uses ranks 0 to 4, up to 5 for video.
concepts.significance: Rank-3 tensors hold sequences and grayscale image batches; rank 4 holds colour image batches; rank 5 holds video (p.50).
concepts.example: `train_images` of shape (60000, 28, 28) is a rank-3 tensor of 60,000 image matrices (p.48).
concepts.misconception: A 'cube' need not have equal sides; (3, 3, 5) is a rectangular block.

math.title: Shape, rank and element count
math.source_text: "Shape—This is a tuple of integers that describes how many dimensions the tensor has along each axis ... the previous matrix example has shape (3, 5), and the rank-3 tensor example has shape (3, 3, 5)"

variables.meaning: Number of entries (dimensions) along axis a.
Rank: the number of axes, equal to the length of the shape tuple.
Total number of numbers stored in the tensor (not stated on the page; added for completeness).

math.operations: Reading the shape tuple; counting its length; multiplying its entries.
math.purpose: Relate the first two key attributes: rank is derived from shape, and shape also tells you how much data the tensor holds.
math.interpretation: Scalar: shape (), rank 0, 1 element. Vector: (5,), rank 1, 5 elements. Matrix: (3, 5), rank 2, 15 elements. Cube: (3, 3, 5), rank 3, 45 elements.
math.intuition: The shape is the tensor's blueprint; everything else about its size follows from it.
math.numerical_example: Beyond the book: with dtype float32 (4 bytes each), the (3, 3, 5) example occupies 45 x 4 = 180 bytes; the MNIST training tensor (60000, 28, 28) as uint8 occupies 47,040,000 bytes ≈ 47 MB, and four times that once cast to float32 on p.44.

math.title: Indexing a rank-3 tensor
math.source_text: the NumPy rank-3 tensor of three packed 3 x 5 matrices; x.ndim -> 3

variables.meaning: Index along axis 0: which of the three packed matrices.
Index along axis 1: which row within that matrix.
Index along axis 2: which column within that row.

math.operations: Three successive selections, one per axis.
math.purpose: Make concrete that rank 3 means three indices, matching the 'cube of numbers' picture.
math.interpretation: Fixing i gives a matrix (a slice of the cube), fixing i and j gives a row vector, fixing all three gives a scalar.
math.intuition: Rank is the number of coordinates needed to locate a cell in the cube.
math.numerical_example: In the page's example all three matrices are identical, so x[0, 1, 3] = x[1, 1, 3] = x[2, 1, 3] = 35, and x[i, 2, 1] = 80 for every i.

code.what_it_does: Shows that the 3 x 5 matrix defined on p.46 has two axes.

line_explanations.explanation: `ndim` of a list-of-lists array is 2: rows along axis 0, columns along axis 1.

code.inputs_outputs: In: the (3, 5) array from p.46. Out: the integer 2.
code.theory_link: Confirms the definition of a matrix as a rank-2 tensor; the shape bullet below gives its shape as (3, 5).

code.title: A NumPy rank-3 tensor
code.what_it_does: Packs three copies of the 3 x 5 matrix into one array, producing a rank-3 tensor of shape (3, 3, 5), and confirms `ndim` is 3.

line_explanations.explanation: Three levels of brackets: the outermost list holds three matrices (axis 0), each matrix is a list of three rows (axis 1), each row a list of five numbers (axis 2). The `...` are interactive continuation prompts, not code.

code.inputs_outputs: In: a list of 3 lists of 3 lists of 5 ints. Out: array of shape (3, 3, 5), 45 elements, `ndim` 3.
code.algorithm: Array construction from a nested sequence; each nesting level becomes an axis.
code.theory_link: Implements 'pack such matrices in a new array' and gives the cube-of-numbers picture; the Shape bullet reads its shape as (3, 3, 5).
pitfalls: All packed matrices must have the same shape; otherwise NumPy cannot form a rectangular tensor.
Using identical matrices is only for brevity; in real data (e.g. MNIST) every slice along axis 0 is a different sample.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: inspect the three key attributes and slice the cube
import numpy as np
m = np.array([[5, 78, 2, 34, 0], [6, 79, 3, 35, 1], [7, 80, 4, 36, 2]])
x = np.array([m, m, m])          # same as packing the three matrices
print(x.ndim, x.shape, x.dtype)  # 3 (3, 3, 5) int64
print(x[0].shape)                # (3, 5): one matrix
print(x[0, 1].shape)             # (5,): one row
print(x[0, 1, 3])                # 35: one scalar
print(x.astype("float32").dtype) # float32

deeper.title: The three attributes on every tensor of the MNIST example
deeper.body:
The page ends by promising to read rank, shape and dtype off the MNIST data. Collecting what the book shows on p.42-48:

| Tensor | rank (`ndim`) | shape | dtype | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `train_images` (as loaded, p.48) | 3 | (60000, 28, 28) | uint8 | 60,000 grayscale 28 x 28 images |
| `train_labels` | 1 | (60000,) | uint8 | one digit per image |
| `train_images` after Listing 2.4 (p.44) | 2 | (60000, 784) | float32 | one flat vector per image, values in [0, 1] |
| `test_images` after Listing 2.4 | 2 | (10000, 784) | float32 | same for the test set |
| `predictions` (p.44) | 2 | (10, 10) | float32 | 10 probability vectors |
| `test_acc` (p.45) | 0 | () | float | a single number |

Every step of the first example changed one of the three attributes deliberately: reshape changed rank and shape, `astype` changed dtype, and the model's layers changed the shape from 784 to 512 to 10.

deeper.title: Why deep learning stops at rank 5
Cube of numbers
deeper.body: The page suggests visualizing a rank-3 tensor as a cube. Picture the 3 x 5 matrix printed on a sheet of paper. Stack three such sheets: you now need to say which sheet, which row and which column to point at a number, three coordinates for a block that is 3 sheets deep, 3 rows tall and 5 columns wide, exactly the shape (3, 3, 5). A rank-4 tensor is a row of such blocks (a bookshelf), rank 5 a wall of shelves. Rank is always the number of coordinates you have to give; shape says how far each coordinate runs; dtype says what is written in each cell.

misconceptions.claim: The shape of a vector with five entries is `(5)`.
misconceptions.correction: It is `(5,)`; in Python `(5)` is just the integer 5. A scalar's shape is the empty tuple `()`.

misconceptions.claim: A rank-3 tensor must be a cube with equal sides.
misconceptions.correction: 'Cube of numbers' is a visual aid; the page's example has shape (3, 3, 5) and MNIST's is (60000, 28, 28). Only the number of axes is fixed at three.

misconceptions.claim: dtype is a property of each element, so a tensor can mix floats and ints.
misconceptions.correction: A tensor has a single dtype shared by all its entries; mixing types forces a conversion to one common type.

misconceptions.claim: Higher rank always means more data.
misconceptions.correction: Rank counts axes, not elements. A (3, 3, 5) rank-3 tensor holds 45 numbers; a (60000, 784) rank-2 tensor holds 47 million.

takeaways: In a matrix, the first axis holds the rows and the second the columns: `[5, 78, 2, 34, 0]` is the first row, `[5, 6, 7]` the first column.
Packing matrices gives a rank-3 tensor (a cube of numbers); packing again gives rank 4, and so on. Deep learning uses ranks 0 to 4, 5 for video.
A tensor is defined by three attributes: rank (`ndim`), shape (a tuple with one size per axis) and dtype.
Shapes: scalar `()`, vector `(5,)`, matrix `(3, 5)`, the page's rank-3 example `(3, 3, 5)`.
Common dtypes are float16, float32, float64, uint8 and bool; TensorFlow also has string tensors.

questions.question: What is the shape of the rank-3 tensor built on this page by packing three 3 x 5 matrices?
questions.explanation: The new packing axis comes first (3 matrices), then the rows (3), then the columns (5), as the Shape bullet states. (9, 5) would be a rank-2 tensor obtained by stacking the rows, not packing the matrices.

questions.question: Name the three key attributes that define a tensor and the NumPy attribute that exposes each.
questions.answer: Number of axes (rank), `ndim`; shape, `shape`; data type, `dtype`.
questions.explanation: The page lists exactly these three; `ndim` is named on the page and `shape`/`dtype` are read off `train_images` on p.48.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly gives the shapes of a scalar and of a 5-entry vector?
questions.explanation: The page states that 'a vector has a shape with a single element, such as (5,), whereas a scalar has an empty shape, ()'. `(5)` is not a tuple in Python, and the other options describe rank-1 or rank-2 tensors of different sizes.

questions.question: In the matrix of p.46, why is `[5, 6, 7]` the first column? Give the index expression that selects it and the one that selects the first row.
questions.answer: The first column consists of the entries at position 0 of every row: 5, 6, 7. It is `x[:, 0]`; the first row is `x[0]` (or `x[0, :]`), equal to `[5, 78, 2, 34, 0]`.
questions.explanation: Rows are entries along axis 0 and columns entries along axis 1; fixing the column index to 0 and taking all rows gives the first column.

questions.question: Explain how the first MNIST example on p.44 changed each of the three key attributes of `train_images`.
questions.answer: `reshape((60000, 28 * 28))` changed the rank from 3 to 2 and the shape from (60000, 28, 28) to (60000, 784); `astype("float32")` changed the dtype from uint8 to float32; dividing by 255 changed the values but none of the three attributes.
questions.explanation: The attributes defined on this page are exactly what the preprocessing of Listing 2.4 manipulated; p.48 confirms the original rank, shape and dtype.

questions.question: Up to what rank do tensors typically go in deep learning, and what kind of data needs the highest rank?
questions.answer: Ranks 0 to 4 are typical; video data needs rank 5.
questions.explanation: Stated directly on the page; p.50 and p.52 show video as (samples, frames, height, width, channels).

questions.question: Given any NumPy array, can you state its rank, shape, dtype and number of elements without running code, just from how it is written? Try it on the page's rank-3 example.
questions.answer: Rank 3 (three bracket levels), shape (3, 3, 5), dtype integer (int64 by default on most platforms), 45 elements.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment on reading the three attributes directly from a literal; the dtype of integer literals is NumPy's platform default integer, a detail not in the book.
